questions.question: In which year was Toxoplasma gondii discovered?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii was discovered in 1908 by Nicolle and Manceaux in the desert rodent Ctenodactylus gundi.

questions.question: Who discovered Toxoplasma gondii?
questions.explanation: Nicolle and Manceaux discovered T. gondii in 1908 at the Pasteur Institute in Tunis.

questions.question: Toxoplasma gondii was first discovered in which animal?
questions.explanation: The parasite was first isolated from the gundi (Ctenodactylus gundi), a desert rodent found in North Africa.

questions.question: The colony where Toxoplasma gondii was first discovered was maintained at which institute?
questions.explanation: The Pasteur Institute in Tunis, Tunisia, is where the original discovery was made.

questions.question: Since the 1980s, Toxoplasma gondii has been recognized as a complicating factor for which patients?
questions.explanation: The HIV/AIDS epidemic since the 1980s brought toxoplasmosis into prominence as a major opportunistic infection in immunosuppressed patients, particularly those with AIDS.

questions.question: Toxoplasma gondii is currently described as what in the human population?
questions.explanation: T. gondii is cosmopolitan — found worldwide. It is one of the most successful parasites on earth, infecting roughly a third of the human population.

questions.question: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular parasite of many kinds of what?
questions.explanation: T. gondii is an obligate intracellular parasite — it must live inside host cells of many kinds of tissues to survive and multiply.

questions.question: Toxoplasma gondii possesses affinities with which group?
questions.explanation: T. gondii has affinities with the coccidia — the intestinal phase of its life cycle in cats resembles that of other coccidian parasites.

questions.question: In heavy acute infections, Toxoplasma gondii can be found free in blood and what else?
questions.explanation: During heavy acute infections, tachyzoites can be found free in the bloodstream and in peritoneal exudates, facilitating systemic spread.

questions.question: Toxoplasma gondii usually lives in which part of the host cell?
questions.explanation: T. gondii typically resides in the cytoplasm of the host cell, in a vacuole of its own making — the parasitophorous vacuole.

questions.question: Intestinal-epithelial development of Toxoplasma gondii occurs in which animal?
questions.explanation: The intestinal-epithelial development (with sexual reproduction) occurs only in cats — the definitive host.

questions.question: Sexual reproduction of Toxoplasma gondii occurs in which host?
questions.explanation: The cat is the definitive host — sexual reproduction (gametogony) occurs in the intestinal epithelium of felines.

questions.question: In hosts other than cats, only what type of reproduction is known for Toxoplasma gondii?
questions.explanation: In all hosts other than cats, only asexual reproduction (endodyogeny) occurs. These hosts are intermediate hosts.

questions.question: Intestinal development in cats begins with ingestion of what?
questions.explanation: Intestinal development in cats begins with the ingestion of tissue cysts (zoitocysts) containing bradyzoites.

questions.question: Asexual generations of Toxoplasma gondii divide by which process?
questions.explanation: Asexual generations divide by endodyogeny — an internal budding process in which two daughter cells form inside the mother cell.

questions.question: Endodyogeny forms how many daughter cells inside the mother cell?
questions.explanation: Endodyogeny produces exactly two daughter cells inside the mother cell before it ruptures.

questions.question: Once inside an epithelial cell of the cat, Toxoplasma gondii becomes what?
questions.explanation: Once inside an epithelial cell, the parasite becomes a trophozoite and begins asexual multiplication.

questions.question: Merogony is multiple fission to produce what?
questions.explanation: Merogony is multiple fission that produces merozoites — this occurs in the intestinal phase in cats.

questions.question: Extraintestinal stages of Toxoplasma gondii begin when a host ingests what?
questions.explanation: Extraintestinal stages begin when a host ingests tissue cysts containing bradyzoites — these invade cells and transform into tachyzoites.

questions.question: Ingested tachyzoites or which other forms are infective?
questions.explanation: Ingested tachyzoites or sporocysts (released from ingested oocysts) are infective and initiate the extraintestinal cycle.

questions.question: In the cat, some sporozoites enter epithelial cells to initiate which cycle?
questions.explanation: In the cat, some sporozoites enter epithelial cells of the intestine to initiate the enteroepithelial cycle — leading to sexual reproduction and oocyst formation.

questions.question: In cells other than those of cats, there is no what development?
questions.explanation: Enteroepithelial development (the sexual cycle) occurs only in cats. In other hosts, only the extraintestinal asexual cycle occurs.

questions.question: Rapidly dividing cells in acute infections are called what?
questions.explanation: Tachyzoites are the rapidly multiplying stage found during acute infection. They are crescent-shaped, multiply by endodyogeny, and cause tissue damage.

questions.question: As infection becomes chronic, slowly multiplying zoites are called what?
questions.explanation: Bradyzoites are the slowly multiplying stage that forms tissue cysts during chronic infection. They persist for life in the host.

questions.question: Toxoplasmosis is caused by which organism?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan parasite.

questions.question: Toxoplasmosis varies in severity from inapparent infection to severe systemic disease terminating in what?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmosis ranges from asymptomatic to severe systemic disease. In its worst form — especially in immunocompromised patients — it causes encephalitis and can be fatal.

questions.question: Man normally acquires Toxoplasma infection by ingesting oocysts from what?
questions.explanation: Oocysts are shed in cat faeces and become infective after sporulation in the environment. Humans acquire infection by ingesting contaminated food, water, or soil.

questions.question: Man acquires Toxoplasma infection by ingesting cysts containing bradyzoites from what?
questions.explanation: Tissue cysts containing bradyzoites are found in raw or undercooked meat — especially pork, lamb, and venison — and are a major source of human infection.

questions.question: The liver and which organ seem to be primary sites of multiplication in human infection?
questions.explanation: After ingestion, the parasite invades the intestinal wall and spreads via the bloodstream. The liver and lungs are the primary sites of multiplication in human infection.

questions.question: Congenital transmission of Toxoplasma may be by which route?
questions.explanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs when tachyzoites cross the placenta during a primary maternal infection. The risk and severity depend on the trimester.

questions.question: Although antibody to Toxoplasma is widely prevalent, clinical toxoplasmosis is what?
questions.explanation: Despite high seroprevalence worldwide (up to a third of humans), clinical toxoplasmosis is rare — most infections are asymptomatic.

questions.question: Which factor contributes to the degree of pathology in toxoplasmosis?
questions.explanation: The age of the host is a significant factor. Older hosts tend to be more resistant, while foetuses and immunocompromised individuals suffer the most severe disease.

questions.question: Older hosts are more what to toxoplasmosis?
questions.explanation: Older hosts are more resistant to toxoplasmosis — they have had more time to develop immunity, and their immune systems have typically been exposed to the parasite already.

questions.question: Symptomatic toxoplasmosis is classified as acute, subacute, chronic, or what?
questions.explanation: Symptomatic toxoplasmosis is classified into four types: acute, subacute, chronic, and congenital.

questions.question: In acute toxoplasmosis, which organ is the first site of infection?
questions.explanation: The intestine is the first site of infection — the parasite invades the intestinal epithelium after being ingested.

questions.question: The first extra-intestinal sites in humans are mesenteric lymph nodes and what?
questions.explanation: From the intestine, the parasite spreads first to the mesenteric lymph nodes and liver parenchyma before reaching other organs.

questions.question: The most common symptom of acute toxoplasmosis is painful, swollen what?
questions.explanation: Lymphadenopathy — painful, swollen lymph glands — is the most common symptom of acute toxoplasmosis.

questions.question: In acute toxoplasmosis, lymph glands are commonly swollen in inguinal, cervical, and which regions?
questions.explanation: Lymphadenopathy in acute toxoplasmosis typically involves the inguinal, cervical, and supraclavicular regions.

questions.question: Subacute toxoplasmosis occurs when immunity in the host develops how?
questions.explanation: Subacute toxoplasmosis occurs when host immunity develops slowly, allowing the parasite to spread and cause more extensive lesions before being controlled.

questions.question: In subacute toxoplasmosis, extensive lesions develop in lung, heart, liver, brain, and what?
questions.explanation: Subacute toxoplasmosis produces extensive lesions in the lungs, heart, liver, brain, and eyes — including the characteristic chorioretinitis.

questions.question: Damage is more extensive in the central nervous system because of lower what?
questions.explanation: The CNS has lower immunocompetence than other tissues — immune cells and antibodies penetrate it less easily — so damage is more extensive there.

questions.question: Chronic toxoplasmosis occurs when immunity builds sufficiently to suppress what?
questions.explanation: Chronic toxoplasmosis occurs when host immunity builds sufficiently to suppress tachyzoite proliferation. The parasite then transforms into bradyzoites and forms tissue cysts.

questions.question: Chronic toxoplasmosis coincides with the formation of what?
questions.explanation: Chronic toxoplasmosis coincides with the formation of tissue cysts — clusters of bradyzoites walled off by the host immune response, persisting for life.

questions.question: Chronic toxoplasmosis may cause myocarditis leading to permanent heart damage and what?
questions.explanation: Chronic toxoplasmosis may cause myocarditis leading to permanent heart damage and pneumonia as the parasite affects the lungs.

questions.question: Congenital toxoplasmosis may cause malformations including hydrocephaly, microcephaly, cerebral calcification, chorio-retinitis, and what?
questions.explanation: Congenital toxoplasmosis causes a classic tetrad — hydrocephalus or microcephaly, cerebral calcification, chorioretinitis, and psychomotor disturbances.

questions.question: Toxoplasma gondii may be isolated by intraperitoneal injection of biopsy material into mice, guinea pigs, or which other animal?
questions.explanation: Isolation can be done by intraperitoneal injection of biopsy material into mice, guinea pigs, or hamsters — susceptible laboratory animals.

questions.question: Which animal is the most suitable medium for culturing Toxoplasma gondii?
questions.explanation: Mice are the most suitable laboratory medium for culturing T. gondii — they are highly susceptible to infection, and the parasite multiplies readily in their tissues.

questions.question: Which serological test is most widely used for detecting antibodies to Toxoplasma gondii?
questions.explanation: The Sabin-Feldman dye test is the most widely used and historically the standard serological test for T. gondii antibodies. It measures specific IgG using live tachyzoites and methylene blue dye.

questions.question: The most convincing method of diagnosing active toxoplasmosis is a four-fold rise in titre coupled with what?
questions.explanation: The most convincing diagnosis of active toxoplasmosis is a four-fold rise in antibody titre combined with isolation of the parasite — either by animal inoculation or culture.

questions.question: The most effective treatment for toxoplasmosis in humans and animals is a combination of pyrimethamine and what?
questions.explanation: The most effective treatment is a combination of pyrimethamine and sulphonamides. These drugs act synergistically by blocking sequential steps in the parasite's folate metabolism.
